title: The Science of Friction on a Rail
bigQuestion: What decides how far a board slides along a ledge before friction stops it?

story.title: Same Speed, Twice as Far
story.kicker: Two skaters hit the same ledge at the same speed, and one slides twice as far.
paragraphs: Deshawn and Ana take turns on a long, low concrete ledge at their neighborhood skatepark. They have both learned the 50-50. They want to know who can grind farther. A friend stands beside the ledge with a tape measure and a phone timer.

To make it fair, they mark a starting line on the ground with chalk and push the same number of times. The friend times each skater over the last two meters before the ledge. Both arrive at about 3 meters per second, a little faster than a jog. Deshawn grinds first and comes off after a little over a meter. Ana grinds the next section of the same ledge and slides about twice as far.

At first they argue about technique. Then Ana points at the edge. Her half of the ledge is shiny with wax. Deshawn's half is bare, rough concrete where the paint has worn away. They switch halves and try again. This time Deshawn goes twice as far, and Ana stops short.

Nothing about the skaters changed. Their speed was the same and their weight hardly mattered. What changed was the surface, and with it the friction between the trucks and the edge. The measuring tape showed a pattern a physicist would recognize: cut the friction in half, and the slide distance doubles.
story.think: The skaters switched halves of the ledge and the results switched too. What does that test tell you about the cause?

lessons.title: What Friction Does
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between two touching surfaces that pushes against the sliding, so it slows a grind.
reading: When metal trucks scrape along a concrete edge, they slow down. The force doing this is *friction*, a force between two surfaces that are touching. Friction always points against the sliding. If the board slides forward along the ledge, friction on the trucks points backward. That backward push is what eventually stops every grind and slide.

Physicists split friction into two kinds. Static friction holds two surfaces still against each other, like the grip between your shoe and the grip tape. Kinetic friction acts while two surfaces slide past each other, like the trucks on a ledge. For most pairs of surfaces, kinetic friction is a bit weaker than the most static friction can give. That is why a stuck board is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

Friction comes from the surfaces themselves. Up close, even a smooth rail has tiny bumps and pits. As the truck slides, those bumps catch, scrape and break, and the surfaces briefly stick together. A rough surface catches more. A slick coating, like wax, fills the pits and lets the surfaces slip. Isaac Newton's first law explains the rest: the board would keep moving if no force pushed against it.

words.d: a force between two touching surfaces that pushes against their sliding
friction that holds two surfaces still against each other
friction that acts while two surfaces slide past each other

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body keeps on in its state of rest, or of moving at a steady speed in a straight line, unless forces acting on it make it change that state.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law I; paraphrased from Andrew Motte's English translation (1729)
look.prompt: Use Newton's first law to explain why a grinding board slows down instead of sliding forever.

check.q: Which way does friction push on a board sliding forward along a ledge?
check.why: Friction always points against the direction of sliding.

check.q: Which kind of friction acts on trucks grinding a ledge?
check.why: Kinetic friction acts while surfaces slide past each other.

check.q: Why does wax lower friction?
choices: it fills tiny pits so surfaces slip past each other
it adds bumps to the rail
check.why: Wax smooths the tiny bumps and pits that catch and scrape.

lessons.title: The Normal Force
lessons.mainIdea: The normal force is the edge pushing up on the board; on a level ledge it equals the skater's weight.
reading: When you stand on a board on a ledge, gravity pulls you down. The ledge pushes back up. That upward push is called the *normal force*. Normal here means at a right angle, because the force points straight out of the surface. On a level ledge, with the skater not bouncing, the normal force exactly balances the weight.

Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass. It equals mass times g, where g is 9.8 meters per second squared near Earth's surface. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons, written N. One newton is about the weight of a small apple. Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same anywhere; weight would change on the Moon.

Here is a worked example. A skater and board together have a mass of 60 kilograms. Weight = m times g = 60 kg times 9.8 m/s squared = 588 N. On a level ledge, the normal force is also 588 N. If the skater pushes down hard or lands from an ollie, the normal force jumps above 588 N for a moment, and so does the friction.

words.d: the push of a surface on an object, at a right angle to the surface
the pull of gravity on a mass; weight = mass times g
the SI unit of force, written N; about the weight of a small apple
how much matter an object has, measured in kilograms

check.q: A skater and board have a mass of 50 kg. What is their weight?
check.why: Weight = 50 kg times 9.8 m/s squared = 490 N.

lessons.title: Friction Equals Mu Times N
lessons.mainIdea: Kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of friction times the normal force: f = μN.
reading: Experiments show a simple pattern for sliding friction. Press two surfaces together twice as hard and the friction roughly doubles. Scientists write this as f = μN. Here f is the friction force, N is the normal force, and μ, the Greek letter mu, is the *coefficient of friction*. The coefficient is a plain number with no unit. It describes how grabby a pair of surfaces is.

The coefficient belongs to a pair of surfaces, not to one. Steel trucks on waxed steel have one value. The same trucks on rough concrete have a larger one. For example, a waxed metal rail might be around 0.2 and bare rough concrete around 0.5. These are example numbers, not fixed constants; real values change with wax, dirt, heat and wear.

Here is a worked example. The 60 kg skater from before grinds a ledge with an example coefficient μ = 0.30. The normal force is 588 N. Friction f = μN = 0.30 times 588 N = 176.4 N, about 176 N. That backward push is a little less than a third of the skater's weight. Notice that the size of the trucks' contact patch does not appear in the formula. For many surfaces, friction depends on the push, not on the area touching.

words.d: a number with no unit, written μ, that tells how strongly two surfaces resist sliding
the rule that kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of friction times the normal force
the small area where two surfaces actually touch

look.title: Amontons and the Load
look.text: Friction between sliding surfaces grows in proportion to the load pressing them together, and it does not depend on how large the touching area appears to be.
look.cite: Guillaume Amontons, report to the French Royal Academy of Sciences, 1699
look.prompt: How does Amontons's finding match the formula f = μN?

check.q: In f = μN, what does N stand for?
check.why: N is the normal force, the surface's push on the board.

check.q: With N = 600 N and μ = 0.25, what is the friction force?
Why is μ = 0.2 for a waxed rail only an example?
choices: real values change with wax, dirt, heat and wear
μ depends on the skater's age
check.why: The coefficient depends on the actual surfaces, so it is a typical value, not a constant.

lessons.title: Slowing Equals Mu Times g
lessons.mainIdea: On a level rail, a grinding board slows at a = μg, so the skater's mass cancels out.
reading: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma. Acceleration is how fast speed changes, in meters per second, each second. When friction is the only push along the ledge, it causes a *deceleration*, a slowing down. Divide the friction force by the mass and you get how quickly the board loses speed.

Put the pieces together. Friction f = μN, and on a level ledge N = mg. So f = μmg. The slowing is a = f divided by m = μmg divided by m. The m on top and the m on the bottom cancel, leaving a = μg. A heavier skater pushes harder on the ledge and gets more friction, but also has more mass to slow down. The two effects cancel exactly.

Here is a worked example. With μ = 0.30, the slowing is a = 0.30 times 9.8 m/s squared = 2.94 m/s squared. Each second, the board loses about 2.94 meters per second of speed. A board that starts the grind at 3.0 m/s stops after t = 3.0 divided by 2.94, about 1.0 second. That matches what skaters see: a grind on a bare ledge lasts about a second unless they bring more speed.

words.d: how fast speed changes, measured in meters per second, each second (m/s squared)
acceleration that slows an object down
Newton's second law: net force equals mass times acceleration

look.title: Light Skater, Heavy Skater
look.text: Picture two skaters on the same waxed ledge, both arriving at 3 m/s. One has a mass of 40 kg with the board, the other 80 kg. The heavier skater presses down twice as hard, so friction on the trucks is twice as big. But the heavier skater also has twice the mass to slow. Both slow at the same rate and stop at about the same spot.

check.q: On a level ledge, what does the slowing of a grind equal?
check.why: a = μmg divided by m = μg, so mass cancels.

check.q: With μ = 0.20, what is the slowing?
check.why: a = 0.20 times 9.8 = 1.96 m/s squared.

check.q: Why do a light and a heavy skater slow at the same rate on the same ledge?
choices: light skaters push the ledge harder
more weight means more friction, but also more mass to slow
gravity is weaker for heavy skaters
check.why: Friction and mass both double together, so the slowing stays the same.

lessons.title: How Far a Grind Goes
lessons.mainIdea: A grind that starts at speed v slides a distance d = v² divided by (2μg) before it stops.
reading: If you know how fast the board starts and how quickly it slows, you can find how far it goes. For steady slowing from speed v down to zero, the *slide distance* is d = v squared divided by 2a. On a level ledge, a = μg, so d = v squared divided by (2μg). Here v is the speed in meters per second as the grind starts.

Here is a worked example, step by step. A skater starts a 50-50 at v = 3.0 m/s on a ledge with an example μ = 0.30. First, square the speed: 3.0 times 3.0 = 9.0. Next, find the bottom: 2 times 0.30 times 9.8 = 5.88. Then divide: d = 9.0 divided by 5.88 = 1.53 meters. The board grinds about one and a half meters before friction stops it.

The formula also works backward. Suppose you want to grind a ledge 2.0 m long with an example μ = 0.25. Solve for v: v squared = 2 times μ times g times d = 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 times 2.0 = 9.8. So v = the square root of 9.8, about 3.1 m/s. Arrive slower than that and the board stops before the end.

words.d: how far a board travels along an edge before friction stops it
the slide distance on a level edge for starting speed v and coefficient μ
to multiply a number by itself; 3 squared is 9

look.title: Working It Out
look.text: Starting speed v = 3.0 m/s. Coefficient μ = 0.30 (an example). Step 1: v squared = 9.0. Step 2: 2 times μ times g = 2 times 0.30 times 9.8 = 5.88. Step 3: d = 9.0 divided by 5.88 = 1.53 m. The trucks stop about a meter and a half down the ledge.
look.prompt: Redo the steps with v = 2.0 m/s. How far does the board go?

check.q: Which formula gives the slide distance on a level ledge?
check.why: The slide distance is v squared divided by 2μg.

check.q: A board starts at 2.0 m/s with μ = 0.20. How far does it slide? (2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92)
check.why: d = 4.0 divided by 3.92 = about 1.02 m.

check.q: What is the first step in the worked example?
check.why: The worked example starts by squaring v: 3.0 times 3.0 = 9.0.

lessons.title: Why Speed Carries a Grind
lessons.mainIdea: Slide distance grows with the square of speed, so doubling your speed makes a grind go four times as far.
reading: Look at the formula again: d = v squared divided by (2μg). The speed is squared. That means distance does not grow in step with speed. It grows much faster. Double the speed and the distance becomes 2 times 2 = 4 times as long. Triple the speed and it becomes 3 times 3 = 9 times as long.

Here is a worked example with μ = 0.30, so 2μg = 5.88. At 1.0 m/s, d = 1.0 divided by 5.88 = 0.17 m. At 2.0 m/s, d = 4.0 divided by 5.88 = 0.68 m. At 4.0 m/s, d = 16 divided by 5.88 = 2.72 m. Going from 2 to 4 m/s, the speed doubled and the distance went from 0.68 m to 2.72 m, four times as far.

This is why skaters say speed is your friend on a long ledge, and why the same idea also calls for care. More speed carries a grind farther, but it also means more energy to manage if the trick goes wrong. A safe plan adds a little speed at a time. If your grind keeps stopping halfway, a small increase in speed often fixes it, because a small change in speed makes a bigger change in distance.

words.d: a pattern where one amount grows with the square of another, so doubling one makes the other four times bigger
how fast something moves, in meters per second
the ability to do work; a moving board has energy that friction must use up to stop it

look.title: Grind Distance at Different Speeds

look.prompt: Compare the 1.0 m/s and 3.0 m/s rows. The speed tripled. About how many times farther did the board go?

check.q: If you double your speed onto a ledge, how much farther does the grind go?
check.why: Distance depends on v squared, and 2 squared is 4.

check.q: In the chart, how far does the board go at 4.0 m/s?
check.why: d = 16 divided by 5.88 = 2.72 m.

check.q: Your grind keeps stopping halfway. What small change does the reading suggest?
check.why: Because distance grows with speed squared, a little more speed carries the grind much farther.

lessons.title: Wax Halves the Mu
lessons.mainIdea: Lowering the coefficient of friction makes a grind go farther; halving μ doubles the slide distance.
reading: In the formula d = v squared divided by (2μg), μ sits on the bottom. When the bottom gets smaller, the answer gets bigger. Cut μ in half and the distance doubles. This is the pattern Deshawn and Ana measured: same speed, same ledge, but the waxed half let the trucks slide about twice as far.

Here is a worked example. Both skaters arrive at 3.0 m/s, so v squared = 9.0. On bare concrete, with an example μ = 0.40, the bottom is 2 times 0.40 times 9.8 = 7.84, so d = 9.0 divided by 7.84 = 1.15 m. On the waxed half, with an example μ = 0.20, the bottom is 2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92, so d = 9.0 divided by 3.92 = 2.30 m. Half the μ, twice the distance.

Wax lowers μ by putting a soft, slippery layer between the metal truck and the hard edge. The truck glides over the wax instead of catching on bumps in the concrete or paint. As skaters grind, the wax gets scraped away and pushed off the ends, so μ creeps back up. That is why the first grinds after waxing feel fast and later ones slow down.

words.d: a soft, slippery coating that lowers the coefficient of friction on an edge
the number μ that tells how strongly two surfaces resist sliding; smaller means slicker
a pattern where one amount gets bigger as another gets smaller

lessons.title: Metal, Concrete and Paint
lessons.mainIdea: Different edges have different friction: smooth metal is usually slick, bare concrete grabs, and paint changes as it wears.
reading: Skateparks build edges from a few materials, and each grinds differently. Many ledges have a *ledge cap*, a strip of steel angle iron along the top corner. Steel is smooth and hard, so trucks slide along it well, and the steel protects the concrete from chipping. Round steel rails and flat bars are also slick, especially after a little wax.

Bare concrete is rougher. Its surface has sand and small stones in it, which catch the trucks and raise the coefficient of friction. Fresh concrete can feel sticky until skaters wear it smooth and wax it. Concrete also crumbles at the corner over time, so a bare edge can get chipped, which makes the board hang up.

Paint changes over time. A newly painted curb can feel slick at first because the paint fills the rough pits in the concrete. As skaters grind it, the paint wears through in patches, and those bare spots grab. For example, a skater may feel the board slow suddenly when the trucks reach a chipped patch. Checking an edge with your hand before skating it is a smart habit.

words.d: a steel strip along the top corner of a ledge that protects it and helps boards slide
a long piece of steel bent into an L shape, often used as a ledge cap
a building material made of cement, sand and small stones that hardens like stone

lessons.title: Heat and Wear
lessons.mainIdea: Friction turns the board's motion energy into heat and wears away the metal, wood and wax it rubs.
reading: A moving board carries *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion, equal to one half times mass times speed squared: KE = ½mv². When friction stops a grind, that energy does not vanish. It turns into *heat* in the trucks and the edge, and a little into sound. That is the rough scraping noise of a grind. Rub your hands together fast and you feel the same effect.

Here is a worked example. A 60 kg skater starts a grind at 3.0 m/s. KE = 0.5 times 60 times 3.0 squared = 0.5 times 60 times 9.0 = 270 joules. A joule is the SI unit of energy. Friction does work equal to force times distance: 176.4 N times 1.53 m = about 270 joules. The two numbers match, because friction used up all the kinetic energy.

Friction also causes *wear*, the slow loss of material from rubbing. Trucks are usually made of aluminum, which is softer than steel, so grinding steel rails shaves tiny amounts off the hangers over time. Slides wear the wood under the nose, tail and middle of the deck. Wax wears off ledges. A worn deck can get thin or chipped, so checking your board for cracks is part of grinding safely.

words.d: the energy of motion; KE = ½mv²
energy that flows as warmth; friction turns motion energy into heat
the SI unit of energy, written J
the slow loss of material from surfaces that rub together

lessons.title: Will It Reach the End?
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the slide distance to the ledge's length tells you whether a grind will make it to the end.
reading: A skater wants to 50-50 a ledge 2.0 m long. The ledge is waxed steel, with an example μ = 0.25. She arrives at 2.5 m/s. Will she reach the end? First, square the speed: 2.5 times 2.5 = 6.25. Next, find the bottom: 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 = 4.9. Then divide: d = 6.25 divided by 4.9 = 1.28 m. That is short of 2.0 m, so the board stops about 0.7 m before the end.

What speed would carry her all the way? Use the formula backward: v squared = 2μgd = 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 times 2.0 = 9.8. The square root of 9.8 is about 3.13. She needs about 3.1 m/s as she starts the grind. That is only about 0.6 m/s more than before, yet it carries her 0.7 m farther.

She has two choices. She can bring a little more speed, or she can lower μ with fresh wax. If wax brings μ down to 0.20, then at 2.5 m/s the bottom becomes 2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92, and d = 6.25 divided by 3.92 = 1.59 m. Wax helps, but here it is not quite enough on its own. A small speed increase is the stronger fix.

words.d: a problem solved step by step to show how a method works
the number that, multiplied by itself, gives a certain value; the square root of 9 is 3
to rearrange a formula to find a starting value, such as the speed needed for a distance

lessons.title: Where the Model Stops
lessons.mainIdea: The formula is a good first model, but real grinds also depend on landing, slope, balance and changing friction.
reading: Every physics formula is a *model*, a simplified picture that matches reality in some ways. The formula d = v squared divided by (2μg) assumes a level edge, a steady μ and a board that slides the whole way. Real grinds break those rules in small ways. Knowing where a model stops helps you use it well.

Landing on the edge is one example. When the trucks hit the ledge after an ollie, the normal force spikes above the skater's weight for a split second. Friction spikes with it, so the board loses extra speed right at the start. Balance is another. If the skater leans and the board tips, the grind ends early, no matter what the formula says.

Slope changes the math too. On a gently sloped flat bar at a skatepark, gravity pulls the board along the slope and partly cancels friction, so the board slows less. On a sloped edge going up, gravity adds to the slowing. The coefficient also changes along a real edge as wax thins and paint wears. Even so, the main ideas hold: more speed and less friction mean a longer grind.

words.d: a simplified picture or formula that matches how something works in some ways
a surface that tilts up or down instead of being level
something a model takes as true to keep the math simple
